key_insight: This paper shows that swallowing-risk in head and neck cancer survivors can be predicted by stacking patient-reported outcome data with clinical information in a two-stage model. The approach aims to flag patients at high risk of dysphagia earlier and more cheaply than relying on videofluoroscopy alone.
problem_solved: Routine dysphagia surveillance after head and neck cancer treatment is difficult because the gold-standard assessment (videofluoroscopic CTCAE-DIGEST) is resource-intensive, requires specialized staff/equipment, and is burdensome for patients. The paper addresses the need for scalable, timely risk stratification in survivorship care.
method: Uses a two-stage PRO-clinical stacking framework to combine patient-reported outcomes with clinical variables.
Learns an intermediate risk representation from PROs, then integrates that signal with clinical data for improved prediction of dysphagia risk.
Targets risk stratification rather than replacing imaging, helping prioritize who should receive more definitive swallow evaluation.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this is a practical example of multimodal clinical prediction that leverages low-cost, high-coverage PROs to augment sparse medical assessments. It highlights how stacked models can improve triage and screening in healthcare workflows where gold-standard labels are expensive or inconvenient.
visual_elements: A pipeline diagram showing PRO inputs, clinical inputs, and the two-stage stacking model.
A simple comparison chart of screening workflow: standard imaging-only vs PRO-clinical risk stratification.
A risk heatmap or patient stratification plot showing low/medium/high dysphagia risk groups.
Icons representing patient survey forms, clinician data, and swallow-imaging assessment.
paper_title: Dysphagia Risk Stratification in Head and Neck Cancer via Two-Stage PRO-Clinical Stacking
paper_authors: Siyuan Zhao, Eric Ababio Anyimadu, Zachary G. Brumm, Yue Ma, Clifton David Fuller
